item.title: Nathaniel Mary Quinn’s Fragments of Home
item.description:
CHICAGO — More than 10 million people in the United States have called public housing home over the past century, yet the country boasts only one museum dedicated to the subject. The National Public Housing Museum (NPHM), after nearly two decades as a roving entity, opened a permanent home in Chicago in early 2025. It seeks to address one of the most intersectional of histories, connecting art, design, architecture, human rights, politics, social policy, the economy, systemic racism, immigration trends, policing practices, and more.

The museum occupies the sole remaining section of the Jane Addams Homes, constructed in 1938 on the southwest side of Chicago. It’s currently surrounded by an empty lot nearly the size of a city block, courtesy the Chicago Housing Authority’s Plan of Transformation, launched back in 1999 to solve the problem of deteriorating buildings, unsafe projects, and racial segregation with widescale demolition and the mostly unfulfilled promise of replacement mixed-income housing for all. That plan eventually amounted to the largest net loss of affordable housing in the country’s history. This story is just one of many told at the NPHM via an engaging combination of archival, experiential, historic, and artistic displays.

The day I visited, offerings included an exhibit devoted to personal objects lent by public housing residents across the country, from a hand-stitched wedding dress and a heavyweight championship belt to an item I found especially relatable, a rotary phone with an extra-long cord. A case study of a rare recent success story, the Millers River Apartments in Cambridge, Massachusetts, nearly broke my head with its meticulous dissection of the impossibly complicated American tax credit system. Especially generous are a pair of apartment units recreating the homes of specific families representative of particular eras: the Turovitzes, Jewish immigrants who were among the first to occupy the Jane Addams Homes, and the Hatches, an African-American couple with eight children who moved in in 1960. A third apartment, set in the 1950s, screens an immersive film explaining what happened in between from a policy perspective, including redlining and racist covenants, via the entrancing silhouette puppetry of the performance collective Manual Cinema.

The museum’s courtyard delights with large limestone animal sculptures, designed by local polymath Edgar Miller for the Jane Addams Homes’ original outdoor play area, now beautifully restored. Also outside are three bang-up works of public art. “Still Here: Zhegagoynak,” a palimpsestic 40-foot-tall (~12.2m) mural by Andrea Carlson, acknowledges the land under the NPHM as being unceded by the Potawatomi. Amanda Williams and Olalekan Jeyifous fashioned an exuberant glass entry portico splashed with colors taken from paint chips left behind when the building’s final residents were forced to move out — vivid hues applied to apartment walls in defiance of Chicago Housing Authority rules mandating beige or light green. Over in the parking lot, Marisa Morán Jahn and Rafi Segal invented new ways to play basketball using a tricycle-mounted hoop system and a radically reimagined court design.

That the NPHM excels in bringing together advanced art and social history comes as no surprise given the credentials of its executive director, Lisa Yun Lee, who has helmed some of Chicago’s most important socially engaged art institutions, from the Hull-House Museum to Open Engagement to the UIC School of Art & Art History. Under her curation, this summer, the NPHM opened Nathaniel Mary Quinn: A Love Letter to My Mother, its first temporary exhibition dedicated to a single artist, also Quinn’s first solo institutional showing in his hometown. Represented by mega-gallery Gagosian and recently in the news for having illustrated the Rolling Stones’ latest album, Quinn grew up in the Robert Taylor Homes on Chicago’s South Side, a place he described as being “incredibly efficient at killing dreams.” His show includes a reading room detailing how the project, the largest in the city and at one point the world, went from Mayor Daley’s proud ribbon-cutting in 1962 to decades of systemic neglect, eroding services, and eventual demolition.

A Love Letter to My Mother is a spare show. Ten portraits on canvas and paper surround a living room meant to evoke Quinn’s family home circa 1984. It was the artist’s first studio, where he sketched directly on the walls; when he ran out of space, his mother washed the old drawings away so he could start anew. At NPHM, each artwork incarnates a person Quinn knew either during his early life or after he moved to Brooklyn as an adult. Extended captions include intimate recollections of his father, a family friend named Junebug, and two flashy guys from his block in Crown Heights. Every one of Quinn’s likenesses is lifelike and demanding of attention, but no one is easy to look at. Fragments of a young neighbor named Erika, her wide dark nose and full lips tenderly rendered, slice sharply into the pale forehead and velvety shoulder of a reproduction of Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (1665). Each segment radiates beauty, but their collision partly blinds the girl, and the proportions fit grotesquely. “Charles: Re-visited," a large bust of the artist’s estranged brother, awkwardly pieces together the fragile mouth and ear of a little boy, the sharp eyes and fedora of a swaggering man, the nose of a bull, a sleeve of streetwear, and an unexpectedly feminine scarf, all in contradictory stylistic registers. The effect unsettles, one aspect obliterating another, the person violently incoherent.

Quinn presents each of his subjects likewise, channeling the critical media mashup of Hannah Höch, the psychological miasma of Francis Bacon, and the rhythmic vitality of Romare Bearden. Arranged from shards, in mismatched angles and aesthetics, their visages look at once battered and lovely, festive and bleak, a human emerging but only just. They hold together via a signature “paint-drawing” technique Quinn has been refining since 2013, resulting in composite portraits that look like collage, down to the edges of white left between what appear to be slices of 17th-century Dutch paintings intercut with slivers of Avedon photographs and bits of anonymous news footage and glossy magazine ads. But, crucially, are not collage, having been crafted seamlessly from a combination of oil paint, charcoal, gouache, paint stick, and pastel. Collage, made of stuck-together scraps originating somewhere else, communicates temporariness, incompleteness, dependence. Quinn’s people comprise multiple parts, under extreme duress, but that is their perennial state. They are not there to be rearranged. 

The Robert Taylor Homes were demolished about two decades ago, long after Quinn left to attend an elite military academy in Indiana on full scholarship. His mother, Mary, died soon after. His family dispersed; he has remained estranged from them ever since. Before graduating, Quinn added Mary’s name to his own so that she, who never finished high school, would also be recognized on his diploma, as she has been on every diploma, honor, collection placard, museum label, gallery announcement, and magazine article — including this one — ever since. It’s a situation of consequent political and philosophical reordering — requiring consideration of a person otherwise relegated to the margins of public life — akin to the realignment aesthetically achieved by Quinn’s portraiture, from which it is equally impossible to turn away.

Nathaniel Mary Quinn: A Love Letter to My Mother continues at the National Public Housing Museum (919 South Ada Street, Chicago, Illinois) through August 23. The exhibition was curated by Lisa Yun Lee.

item.title: Divers Stumble Upon 2,000-Year-Old Roman Shipwreck in Italy
item.description:
While exploring the warm waters of the Sicilian coast last week, two Italian divers discovered hundreds of clay vessels piled atop an approximately 2,000-year-old Roman shipwreck.

In an Instagram post chronicling the discovery, Giacomo De Mola recalled finding the site with his diving partner, Igor Bisulli, after mistaking the wreck for a "big rock."

Sicilian cultural authorities clarified in a statement that the ship resides at a depth of 46 meters (151 feet) and primarily carries Dressel 1A amphorae (named after the German archaeologist Heinrich Dressel), late Roman Republic ceramic wine jars characterized by their angularity, pointed base, and collared rim. The divers also unearthed two anchor stumps and an unidentifiable lead structure.

"The discovery is, to me, now very exciting," De Mola told Hyperallergic. "I did not expect it to be so important."

Italian Minister of Culture Alessandro Giuli described the site in a statement to Hyperallergic as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years."

Underwater photos of the discovery, which De Mola shared with Hyperallergic, show piles of amphorae overgrown with sea life. In each image, the signature vessel shape remains prominent, with glimpses of the original red clay base peeking through thick crusts of barnacles and vegetation. Dated between the second and first centuries BCE, the wreck could provide further insights into Ancient Rome's war-torn expansion throughout the Mediterranean.

De Mola speculated that the wreck could also contain Lamboglia 2 amphorae, along with clay jars from Neo-Punic-era North Africa. Sicilian authorities have not yet disclosed the classifications of the amphorae and their contents.

The discovery recalls other ancient Roman shipwreck findings in recent years. In 2019, over 300 amphorae were found in the hull of a 1,700-year-old vessel in Mallorca. Two years later, another collection of amphorae was discovered off the coast of Palermo.

"The sea never ceases to amaze us," De Mola wrote on Instagram. "This time we didn’t find just a wreck. We found a piece of our history."

item.title: RIP Vermeer, You Would’ve Hated AI
item.description:
Every book is a record of the life of the people who thumbed through it, the binder who secured its pages in place, the designers who chose its cover and typeset. So, when news emerged that Anthropic scanned and destroyed out-of-print titles to train Claude, it felt like a gut-punch to the very spirit of storytelling and artmaking that has always sustained our humanity.

This week, author Ed Simon articulates the fascist logic behind this destruction, and reminds us why we must keep reading, writing, and critiquing in the face of it. Writer Natasha Seaman, for one, had mixed feelings about a new book on Vermeer, who has amassed a devoted following in part because his personal history still largely remains a mystery. Read her sharp review of the biography below, plus the latest in art book news.

As for me, I’m counteracting the technocracy’s affront on books by revisiting old favorites (Pride & Prejudice, yes, I am an Austenphile) and discovering new ones (Valeria Luiselli’s Beginning Middle End and Jennifer Higgie’s Bedlam). Put that in your algo and smoke it, Anthropic.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity

After Spanish physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake in 1553 for religious heresy, only three surviving copies of his The Restoration of Christianity would be spared from the bonfire. One particular copy, now held by the University of Edinburgh library, is ironically believed to have been personally saved by the Protestant leader John Calvin, who was responsible for Servetus’s execution in Geneva. Anyone familiar with Calvin, who bragged in a letter that he had “purged the Church of so pernicious a monster,” knows that the book wasn’t preserved due to affection for Servetus, but rather a bibliophile’s sentiment — even a doctrinaire, zealous, tyrannical bibliophile.

And yet, as bizarre as Calvin’s motivations might have been, he’s still not as noxious as the artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, that have been involved in bulk purchasing, digitizing, and then pulping out-of-print books to train their large language models. Calvin at least had the excuse of his God; AI companies don’t even have that. | Ed Simon

Read More

From Our Critics

The Fruitless Search for Vermeer’s Personal God

A recent biography spends too much time speculating about the Dutch artist’s religious beliefs and not enough exploring other mysteries, including his possible use of a camera obscura. | Natasha Seaman

Read More

News From the Book World

  • The German publishing giant Steidl Verlag, known for photobooks by leading artists including Nan Goldin, Gordon Parks, Walker Evans, and Joseph Beuys, is facing an uncertain future after coming close to bankruptcy.

Member Comment

It’s gotten to be that Hyperallergic is the most important thing I read every day. I thank this publication for the work it does.

As someone tasked with the liquidation of an artist’s estate, I can tell you that many, many beautiful books are going to go into the trash this year, without the help of the marauding industries of AI. Library simply do not want book donations, as a rule.

—Sally Eckhoff on "AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity"

The History of Blackness Is Entwined With Blue

item.title: Divers Discover Hundreds of Ancient Ceramic Vessels Amid Shipwreck Off the Coast of Sicily
item.description:
Divers with a specialized unit of the Carabinieri, Italy’s military police, have uncovered a 2,000-year-old shipwreck on the ocean floor off the northwest coast of Sicily. In a Facebook post on August 7, Alessandro Giuli, Italy’s culture minister, said that this is “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries in recent years.”

According to the BBC, local fishermen alerted the Carabinieri to the shipwreck, which was full of hundreds of ancient Roman vessels called amphorae. The boat itself is nearly 70 feet long and 20 feet wide, and was discovered at a depth of 150 feet.

Italian spearfisherman and freediver Giacomo De Mola posted a video on Instagram on August 8 describing “without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life.” De Mola recounts that he and a friend, Igor Bisulli, were scanning the seabed off the coast of Mazara del Vallo with their StructureScan, which uses sonar technology to view underwater terrain in 3D. What he thought was a large rock turned out to be an ancient ship full of hundreds of pieces of well-preserved pottery. There are also two anchors and a lead pipe. “It is hard to describe the feeling of being among the first humans in nearly twenty centuries to see that place again,” De Mora wrote.

 In a statement, the Carabinieri designated the location of the shipwreck as a “significant underwater archaeological site” and explained that the site will undergo detailed documentation and study overseen by the Superintendency of the Sea.

item.title: National Gallery of Art Protects Works Ahead of Trump's IndyCar Race
item.description:
An IndyCar race taking place in the nation’s capital later this month as part of President Trump's “Freedom 250” celebrations is under scrutiny as experts study the possible impact of race car vibrations on thousands of artworks held in museum collections near the track.

The National Gallery of Art (NGA), one of several institutions located on the 1.7-mile Freedom 250 Grand Prix circuit — along with the Hirshhorn Museum, the National Archives, and the National Museum of the American Indian, and others — conducted a study to examine possible consequences “out of a great abundance of caution,” a spokesperson said.

“Based on the results, we have implemented a set of measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection, and facilities during the race,” the NGA spokesperson told Hyperallergic in a statement, noting that the museum is not disclosing specific findings.

According to the New Republic, some artworks at the Washington, DC, museum have been reinstalled to face away from the side of the building that faces the racetrack. Further images from the Washington Post showed that some outdoor artworks had been boarded up, including I.M. Pei's skylights in front of the museum's East building.

A White House spokesperson told Hyperallergic that the White House and IndyCar's parent company, Penske Corporation, "have followed all appropriate protocols and been in close coordination with all relevant agencies to ensure this is also the safest and most secure race for all visitors to enjoy.” (Penske Corporation is owned by Republican donor Roger Penske, who is the father of Jay Penske, founder of Penske Media Corporation.)

item.title: Ireland’s Museum Staffers Struggle with Precarious Contracts and Toxic Environments
item.description:
Museum staffers in Ireland are finding it increasingly difficult to sustain a career in the field over unstable contracts, low pay and toxic working environments, according to Dr. Emma McAlister, who wrote a blog post on the issue for the International Council of Museums on Monday.

As McAlister recounted, she has only been able to work in the Irish museum industry over the last two and a half years through a temporary rolling contract that, at times, would be renewed just one day before its expiration. Her experience isn’t isolated.

A 2024 compensation study from the lobby group Irish Museums Association found there was an overreliance on temporary contracts and volunteers in the country’s museums. Around 52 percent of museum workers were on permanent or rolling contracts with volunteers making up their second largest pool, standing at 27 percent, IMA said in the report. Only 6 percent of workers were on fixed-term contracts for up to five years. The transition from short-term contracts to permanent positions is a fundamental issue Ireland’s museums need to address, the IMA concluded in its report.

Temporary contracts add to instability, McAlister wrote, and create a culture of silence around employee mistreatment and toxic hierarchies. Ireland’s museums in particular have a reputation for unhealthy working cultures, she wrote. For instance, one in five workers were “often” bullied at the National Museum of Ireland, according to a previous Irish Times report.

Due to the prestigious nature of these cultural institutions, there’s an “expectation of gratitude” despite low pay and toxic hierarchies. This is not just limited to museums in Ireland. In the UK, 16 percent of staffers working in cultural activities were paid below living wage in 2024, according to the Museums Association, a UK-based membership organization for museum, gallery and heritage professionals and organizations.

One underlying issue that results in museum staffers being underpaid with fragile job security lies in the underfunding of the museum sector. But some governments have pledged recent investments into established and local museums as a means to boost the sector.

On Friday, Ireland’s Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, Patrick O’Donovan earmarked €274,000 ($316,000) for local and regional museums in the country. Meanwhile, Northern Ireland’s Ulster Folk Museum also received £40 million ($54 million) in government funding.

Ireland’s funding boost follows the UK’s £1.5 billion pledge over a five-year time period, £600 million of which will be pledged to Department-funded museums, such as the British Museum and the National Portrait Gallery, while £160 million has been pledged for regional and local institutions.

While further government funding is a positive signal the museum sector could be moving in the right direction, it isn’t yet clear how the new budgets will be used by individual museums, and if some of the new funds will be directed toward staff retention.

Fundamentally, the Irish museum sector needs to “face a long-overdue reckoning” with help from governments and funding bodies, McAlister said.

item.title: How Betye Saar Came to Be
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — There is an African Adinkra symbol, “Sankofa,” that means “go back and get it.” It’s intended to preach the importance of looking to the past when shaping the future, and to share wisdom between generations. On the occasion of her 100th birthday, Roberts Projects in Los Angeles organized an exhibition to recognize the earliest professional works of Betye Saar — the prolific assemblage artist who prodded the psyche of the Black American experience for over seven decades before her death last month. The show sheds light on a lesser-known facet of her canon: costume design. 

Through the over 200 archival objects in the show, one gets a good sense of the multiple pots Saar had her fingers in at the beginning of her career. Costume design, dancing (a full-wall photo of a young dancing Saar acts as the exhibition greeter), photography, drawing, jewelry, garments, greeting cards, album covers, and more are on view. The range depicts Saar’s broad curiosities, but it also underlines her particular skill in identifying various potentials and fitting them together. 

Some of the first archival photographs in the show are costume and set designs for a 1970 production of Antigone at the Inner City Cultural Center (ICCC), then located at the intersection of Washington and Vermont in Los Angeles. Saar worked on the costumes for the play but also did the backgrounds; the wallpaper was her first foray into collage work. “I just love materials,” Saar said during a press walkthrough of the show. “This was one of the first times I really got to play with that sort of collage work long before I knew what assemblage was.” 

In fact, this entire exhibition is an ode to Saar discovering the practice of mixing media for which she would become internationally recognized. In her costume work, she reimagined second-hand clothes into abstract garments for the stage or gathered found materials to fashion into accessories. Her sketches and fabric swatches are displayed in vitrines underneath photos of the designs in situ. With certain productions, she explained during the walkthrough, she would “often break down some of the stage work to a smaller scale to sell in the gift shop.” That idea is reminiscent of her classic assemblage work “Black Girl’s Window” (1969), made around the same era. In addition to the early costumes, the exhibition highlights Saar’s domestic creations for her three daughters — Lezley, Alison, and Tracye (plus Tracye’s stuffed bear “Tutti”) — and homemade outfits for the very first years of the Renaissance Pleasure Faire.

item.title: Looted Ivorian “Talking Drum” Arrives at Its Home Village After More Than a Century
item.description:
A sacred “talking drum” known as the Djidji Ayôkwé, looted from Côte d’Ivoire by French colonial troops over a century ago, returned this month to the place where it was made. According to the Namibia Press Agency (NAMPA), the drum arrived on August 7 at its home village of Adjame, where the local community was able to see it for the first time.

The ten-foot-long, 940-pound drum has a single-piece cylindrical soundbox slit in half longitudinally. Extending out from the slit are two planks, one of which supports a carving of a jumping leopard. The box itself is decorated with carved and painted faces and geometric patterns.

The massive instrument was once used by Côte d’Ivoire’s Atchan/Ebrié people to transmit messages between villages many miles apart, including warnings of impending French recruitment operations. It was seized by colonial authorities in 1916 as a way of suppressing local resistance.

Between 1916 and 1930, the Djidji Ayôkwé was kept outside the French governor’s Ivorian home. It was transferred to France in 1929 and housed most recently at Paris’s Musée Quai Branly, where it recently underwent restoration.

The drum topped a list of 148 objects that Côte d’Ivoire requested from France in 2019; the petition followed French President Emmanuel Macron’s 2017 pledge to return works of art looted in Africa during the colonial era.

Following a 2025 vote by the French parliament to authorize its repatriation, the Djidji Ayôkwé was handed over to the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire in a ceremony at the Musée Quai Branly in February. It arrived in Côte d’Ivoire in March but had not been taken out of its crate until now.

Ensconced in a glass case mounted on a float, the drum was paraded through the Yopougon district of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire’s largest city, before continuing on to Adjame. There it was met by Ivorian minister of culture Francoise Remarck, along with local dignitaries and residents.

“A nation cannot develop if it doesn’t preserve its memory and promote its heritage,” Adjame mayor Farikou Soumahoro said.

“We want to see the drum with our own eyes so we can truly believe it belongs to us,” said villager Jacqueline Akrebie.

Traditional leader Cyriaque Ahoure said he had come to share a moment of “great joy, when we remember our ancestors.”

The drum will be exhibited at the Museum of Civilizations in Abidjan.

In recent years, institutions and collectors in the U.S. and Europe have faced increasing pressure to return cultural property to its original communities. In April, France passed a new law facilitating the restitution of items illegally acquired between 1815 and 1972.

item.title: Family Memories and Midwestern Niceties Converge in Melissa Joseph’s ‘Casserole Culture’
item.description:
Unlike the coasts, Midwestern culture is synonymous with the manual labor of blue-collar jobs, resilience necessary in harsh winters, and a certain friendliness that lends itself to a deep-rooted sense of community. These humble tenets grounded Melissa Joseph’s childhood in Saint Marys, a small, rural city in Pennsylvania, where she was born to a mother with Irish heritage and a father from Kerala, India. The melange of biracial life, Midwestern niceties, and gendered fiber art traditions are woven through Joseph’s artistic practice, which translates family photos into tender needle-felted scenes.

In her forthcoming solo exhibition, Casserole Culture, the New York-based artist echoes the warmth and mundanity present in these snapshots of life through soft layers of wool. An upturned hat on a wooden dresser, the bright orange flowers of dining room wallpaper, and even the titular hot dish all appear in hazy fiber, nodding to the fuzziness of memory.

Alongside two-dimensional works, Joseph also incorporates found objects like worn tires, salvaged boxes, frames, and industrial materials into her more sculptural pieces. In this body of work, a felted fire roars inside a hulking model hearth, for example, while another embeds a fragment of a fork inside a metal-and-wood form.

The artist’s mother died in 2024, and she’s found it difficult to depict her family in the wake of such profound grief, instead focusing on their possessions and the places where cherished moments occurred. “Even if the people themselves may elude the artist’s hand, she captures the spaces they enliven, the unremarkable yet prized moments that shape our lives,” says a statement about the exhibition.

Casserole Culture will be on view from September 9 to October 17 at Charles Moffett in New York. Until then, explore more of Joseph’s work on Instagram.

item.title: Three Public Artworks by Banksy Have Cost UK Taxpayers Almost $200,000
item.description:
Banksy’s guerrilla artworks have generated millions of dollars in auction sales and drawn crowds wherever they appear. They’ve also left British taxpayers footing a growing cleanup bill.

Public authorities across London have spent nearly $203,000 removing, protecting, and managing three of the anonymous street artist’s works since 2024, according to figures obtained by the BBC through Freedom of Information requests. The total will keep going up as officials continue efforts to erase one of the artist’s latest murals from the walls of London’s Royal Courts of Justice last year.

The work, depicting a judge in a wig striking a protester with a gavel, has cost Britain’s Ministry of Justice $67,000 in removal efforts so far, with another $48,000 spent on security and staff overtime while the work stayed up. Contractors now are using laser technology after initial cleaning attempts failed, and officials have said that replacing the affected stonework might be the next step if those efforts are unsuccessful. 

The mural has reignited a familiar debate over whether Banksy’s modus operandi should be treated as criminal vandalism or culturally significant public art. Critics, including Britain’s Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy, argued taxpayers should not bear the cost of cleaning what he described as damage to a national symbol of the rule of law. Others defended the work, saying Banksy’s murals attract visitors and make art accessible outside traditional museums and galleries. 

The court mural is only the latest example.

In April, Westminster City Council said it spent nearly $81,000 on safety barriers, security, and administrative costs after Banksy secretly installed a statue in Waterloo Place near Trafalgar Square. The council, which became the legal owner of the sculpture because it sits on public land, said it is still considering what to do with the work. 

Earlier, in August 2024, the City of London removed a police sentry box that Banksy had transformed with painted piranha fish at a cost of almost $3,000. Rather than being relegated to the scrap yard, the structure was placed into storage and is scheduled to go on public display when the London Museum reopens in November.

item.title: Fossils and Other Exhibits Stolen From German University in Latest Museum Robbery
item.description:
The University of Bonn in Germany announced last week that numerous fossils and other exhibits have been stolen from its Goldfuß Museum. The university is now appealing to the public for information on items put up for sale or found on display, in order to secure their recovery.

The university said it is not clear when the items were stolen, but that it occured during renovation work, which began in December 2023 and is ongoing. In a blog post published August 7, the university shared images of the missing items, and asked the public for assistance.

“Anyone who has spotted one of the items shown, seen them being offered for sale—e.g. online, on fossil shows, trading platforms or in a store—or noticed anything else that might be relevant is asked to contact the Bonn Police without delay,” the blog post reads, directing the public to send tips to Bonn Police’s Criminal Investigation Division.

The university “strongly advise[d]” people not to contact the sellers on their own, but to pass along detais.

“Besides the damage caused to the museum building and the theoretical market value of individual items, however, the theft also represents a loss of considerable intellectual significance, as every exhibit stolen from the historical collection, which stretches back to the institute’s founder Georg August Goldfuß (1782—1848), can now no longer be used for research or teaching purposes,” the blog post continues.

Per a separate FAQ, the university said that the theft was discovered after certain wooden safety enclosures were due to be dismantled. Workers found the cases broken into and the items, detailed in photos, missing.

The incident is just the latest theft at a major museum in Europe. While last October’s brazen daylight Louvre robbery has captured headlines and public attention, there have numerous robberies since, including an all-night robbery in Italy in late July in which thieves made off with $4.63 million worth of art.

item.title: Inhotim Founder Bernardo Paz to Open a Namesake Museum, Right Next Door
item.description:
Brazil’s Minas Gerais will soon see another museum thanks to mining magnate Bernardo Paz, the megacollector behind the Inhotim museum and nature complex. The Museu Bernardo Paz will turn 311 acres of countryside into a new landscape for “art, nature and community.” The first phase will open in September 2027. 

“Museu Bernardo Paz is taking root and flourishing from a belief in the creative potential of unexpected encounters,” said Paz in press materials. “This is a place to discover new relationships between art and landscapes of different kinds, between artists and audiences that have not yet met one another, and between the community of Brumadinho and visitors from all over the world. All of this is coming together here, and all of it is for the people.”

The museum will encompass more than 20 galleries and pavilions, with commissioned outdoor installations and sculptures, all set in a landscape that includes a lush botanical park and a forest. Locals will be able to take advantage of a community center with a library and art studios. One of the pavilions in development will be devoted to music and dancing, “essential elements of Brazilian culture and identity,” according to the organizers.

The first phase will include pavilions dedicated to the work of Laura Belém, Sandra Gamarra, Sonia Gomes, Michael Heizer, Anna Maria Maiolino, and Pedro Moraleida, as well as major large-scale sculptures and environments by Torkwase Dyson, Frida Orupabo, Giuseppe Penone, and Mario Garcia Torres. Heizer’s pavilion, the first permanent installation in Latin America, is in progress, and will be dedicated to two large-scale 1993 installations, Displaced Replaced Mass #3 and Negative Wall Sculpture #1.

“At a moment when there is a prevailing global sense of ever-narrowing possibilities—whether in culture, society, the environment, or politics—we hope that Museu Bernardo Paz will be a place that renews the imagination,” said Paulo Miyada, artistic director, in the press release. “In a landscape full of conjunctions that challenge established notions of museum and landscape, intense opportunities emerge for creation, inspiration, and transformation.”

Paz, who has frequently ranked on the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list, co-founded Inhotim in 2006 with New York art advisor Allan Schwartzman, who is also chief curatorial advisor on the new museum. Residing on a 700-acre campus, the museum mixed art, some of it new commissions, with nature preserves and imported flora. It features major pieces by a who’s-who of contemporary art, including international figures such as Doug Aitken, Matthew Barney, Chris Burden, Yayoi Kusama and David Lamelas, as well as Brazilian artists including Cildo Meireles, Hélio Oiticica, Lygia Pape, Valeska Soares, and Adriana Varejão.

The new museum complex in the Brumadinho region will also feature some 15,000 trees and a million shrubs, cacti, and flowering plants in a design inspired by Paz’s relationship with 20th-century landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx. Striking arrangements of fruit trees and flowering trees are promised for a space that borders the Inhotim Private Natural Heritage Reserve and the Paz Environmental Protection Area. 

“Bernardo Paz opened up unprecedented possibilities for contemporary art museums when he founded Inhotim 20 years ago,” said Schwartzman. “With that landmark institution now established, he is moving beyond it into new experimental territory. There is a creative abundance at Museu Bernardo Paz—a distinctive and radical sense of discovery—that will be astonishing in both scope and imaginative force.”

In 2017, Paz was sentenced to nine years in jail for money laundering related to Inhotim, but the decision was reversed in 2020.

item.title: ‘Remember Me’ Highlights Black Americans’ Self-Expression in Early Photography
item.description:
In our era of screens and proliferous imagery, it strains the imagination to comprehend a time before photography. Two centuries ago, an inventor named Nicéphore Niépce took the very first picture of his courtyard in France by fitting a pewter plate into a camera obscura. A few years later, a professional scene painter named Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre conceived of the aptly named daguerreotype, in which the image could be permanently fixed. He and Niépce both sold their technologies to the French government, which then published a how-to guide and facilitated the global spread of the process. In 1939, the first daguerrotypes were created in the U.S.

As they say, the rest is history. Except, we often only see a part of the whole story. Because the technology was expensive, and therefore having your photograph taken (let alone owning the equipment) was costly, the visual record of the 19th century in this medium is heavily skewed toward affluent, white individuals and families who could afford it. Due to the long exposure time required to capture the images, we also don’t see candid shots, as carefully posed scenes were required for clarity and fidelity.

Photography was invented decades before the Civil War and the end of slavery in the U.S., yet so rarely do we glimpse real faces that “illuminate the complexities of race, freedom, and agency before, during, and after the Civil War,” says the National Gallery of Art, which presents Remember Me: Picturing African Americans in Early Photography later this year. The exhibition brings forward dozens of images taken of and by Black Americans, showcasing a wide variety of lived experiences in one place.

Fashion, family, and social status are on full display in a range of gelatin silver prints, daguerrotypes, tintypes, and ambrotypes, some of which are colorized. Because many of the earliest formats were very fragile, they were often displayed in ornate folding cases. Several of these will be included with their images, plus cabinet cards and portraits by pioneering Black artists like James Van Der Zee, who ran a prominent studio in Harlem in the early 20th century.

The exhibition will highlight around 70 pieces in the museum’s collection that center self-expression and the entrepreneurial spirit of African American individuals. Remember Me is slated to open on November 7 and will continue through March 14 in Washington, D.C. Learn more and plan your visit on the museum’s website.

item.title: The Native History of NYC's Oysters
item.description:
The oyster, writes Hrag Vartanian, is "no incidental New Yorker, but perhaps its most symbolic creature." Hyperallergic's co-founder and editor-at-large visits Mohawk artist Alan Michelson’s poetic installation in Governor’s Island, where about a million oyster shells culled from Manhattan restaurants stir reflections on Native land and historical memory. Vartanian muses on the glorious mollusk’s history, from Lenape shell middens to NYC’s menus to the detrimental effects of their disappearance on our ecosystems. In Michelson’s work, Vartanian writes, “the shells become forces of insurgency, counter-experts that quietly refute settler innocence and its alibi that ‘nothing was here’ before extraction.”

Still can’t get a ticket for Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey in New York? Welcome to the club. Here’s a cooler plan: Head uptown to The Met to see a rare, 2,300-year-old fragment with lines from Homer’s epic, now on view at the museum. No hot takes about the historical accuracy of Bronze Age armor required. Papyrus > IMAX.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

The Lost Pearls of New York City

Walking down Pearl Street in Manhattan’s Chinatown, you probably don’t realize that the name marks the original 17th-century East River shoreline of New York City. In fact, the street was named for a Lenape shell midden that was located on its southern section, which is also believed to have been adjacent to a Lenape canoe landing. It was one of many prominent middens that marked the region, and as Mark Kurlansky explains in his bestselling book The Big Oyster: History on the Half Shell (2006), middens are “the most common marker of a pre-European settlement anywhere in the area of the mouth of the Hudson.” These piles of oyster shells, he notes, were sometimes as much as four feet deep, sometimes buried in the ground, sometimes piled high. | Hrag Vartanian

item.title: Joeun Kim Aatchim’s Layered Lines Summon Translucent Worlds
item.description:
In Joeun Kim Aatchim’s paintings—but she calls them drawings—everything is so vivid, yet so elusive. Her line feels definitive, yet the images they convey seem to fade away into sheer luminosity. 

Her works are typically painted using mineral pigment in shellac—sometimes with watercolor, pastel, or other materials—on layers of silk that, stretched across frames, show through to the wall behind. They’re all about one image being seen through another—not different things, in the manner of Francis Picabia’s transparencies, but different versions of the same thing; different attempts, a little like the way Henri Matisse would partially overpaint his works to show multiple thoughts about how to depict one thing, or how to position it within the composition. 

Aatchim speaks about her method as being a layering of first drafts. “Rather than working on a piece over and over to make it perfect,” she told me, “I can keep my first thought” even as the piece develops. The result is a bouquet of essays, finding resolution in the tentative. She calls what she does “drawing” because she considers it “a thought in progress,” and because her materials never completely cover the surface she’s working on. “It doesn’t matter if it’s pencil or chalk or paint. If it doesn’t cover the surface, I consider that a drawing, whether it’s on the floor, on the street, or on the wall, or an object.”

The Korean-born artist has been exhibiting widely since earning her MFA at Columbia University in 2017, where she’d gone at the suggestion of Kiki Smith, to whom she’d been an assistant. Since then, she’s had solo shows at galleries in New York, Los Angeles, Guadalajara, Seoul, and Madrid. Coming later this year is her first exhibition in São Paulo, at Almeida & Dale. I caught up with Aatchim not in her Brooklyn studio but in Seoul, by Zoom, while she was visiting her parents. Was she working there? “I tried to rest, but I don’t know how to rest, and I don’t have any hobbies,” she said. “I started thinking, maybe I’m nobody if I’m not making art. So I started making work in the dining room.” In any case, she added, the materials she likes to use are more readily available in Korea than in New York.

But maybe, her real material is mnemonic. She considers her vivid sense of recall to be both a blessing and a curse. She explains that “memories I haven’t drawn yet keep lingering in my head, and have to be stored somewhere. You know, because I stored this somewhere safe, I can now get new memories.” That probably explains why her simple yet multilayered portraits of friends and observations of her everyday world can be at once so clear and distinct yet so intangible. After all, memories can’t be fixed. They’re always thoughts in progress.

item.title: New York Socialite Tracey Amon Asks Court to Compel Advisor Sandy Heller to Turn Over Papers Connected to Late Ex-Husband’s Art Collection
item.description:
New York’s Tracey Amon filed a request on July 25 in the US District Court for the District of Southern New York to subpoena art advisor Sanford “Sandy” Heller. She wants him to turn over documents for use in her lawsuits in Switzerland over the disposition of the assets of her late husband, Maurice Alain Amon, who retained Heller as an advisor starting in 2013. Heller has been described as “possibly the biggest art advisor in the world,” and reputedly works with Roman Abramovich and Steve Cohen.

The heir to the company SIPCA, which makes inks used in printing currency, Maurice died at 68 in 2019 while on holiday in Saint Tropez. The filing puts his value at some $600 million in assets and business interests at the time of his death, and asserts that Tracey is looking for her rightful share. The request revolves around Heller’s valuation of the collection.

The two married in Hong Kong in 2008 “without signing a marriage contract on that occasion or later,” according to an exhibit. He filed abroad for divorce in 2015 without telling her, says the filing, which claims he secretly removed some 20 artworks, collectively valued at $25 million, from their New York home. He allegedly also spirited away artworks from other residences. He claimed in court filings in 2017 that after losing her key, she took a blowtorch to a lockbox in their Paris home, allegedly leaving a toxic dust over artworks by the likes of Jean-Michel Basquiat, Damien Hirst, Richard Prince, Gerhard Richter, Cy Twombly and Andy Warhol.

While the divorce was in process, he allegedly executed a will naming Albert Amon, his son from a previous marriage, as his only heir, and his assistant, Silvio Venturi, as executor. The New York Post reported that in 2018, she had won about $123,000 a month in spousal support and a lump sum of about $1.3 million in a Monaco court. He allegedly added other legatees and beneficiaries in a codicil executed in Singapore in 2019. She sued Albert and Venturi in Switzerland in 2020; they also brought an action against her.

The Justice of the Peace in Lausanne ordered the administration of the estate in December 2024. Administrator Olivier Weniger issued an inventory in December 2025, along with a report from accounting firm KPMG with an evaluation of the art holdings as of 2019 of Artmon, the holding company through which Amon held his artworks, which was registered in the British Virgin Islands. 

“It appears that the value of Artmon’s artworks diminished dramatically during 2019,” says the filing, adding, “This diminution appears to be based at least partially on Heller’s valuation.” Heller reported capital losses of €33.4 million and latent capital gains of €7.5 million, for a loss of about €26 million, or $29.6 million. “But,” says the filing (in bold type and italics), “there is no list of the works Heller actually examined, no methodology provided, and no information as to when Heller did its evaluation.”

Heller did not immediately return a request for comment.

Tracey Amon is seeking the complete valuation report and all associated work product, including the list of artworks examined, comparables considered, the valuation methodology, and all relevant correspondence. She also seeks documentation of all of Heller’s dealings with Artmon and the Maurice Amon estate, including any art sales, art purchases, consignments, inventories, invoices, and the like.

The court has yet to respond to Amon’s request.

item.title: 2,300-Year-Old Fragment of Homer’s “Odyssey” Now on View at The Met
item.description:
The subway trek to the Upper East Side is slightly easier than Odysseus's journey across the Mediterranean, provided the 6 train is running. For those who prevail, their reward will be plentiful: A 2,300-year-old papyrus fragment containing parts of Homer's Odyssey is now on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The institution announced this week that the object would emerge from its long retirement on August 5. The fragment is now on public view at the museum in Gallery 162.

In a video accompanying The Met's announcement, Séan Hemingway, curator in charge of Greek and Roman art, described the papyrus as “the earliest preserved fragment of Homer's Odyssey that we have today.”

item.title: Could This New Legislation Protect Historic Sites From Trump's Wrath?
item.description:
As President Donald Trump and his appointees escalate their legislative attacks against historic sites and the artworks housed within them, Democrats and preservationist groups are pushing for protective countermeasures.

On July 24, the heavily Trump-appointed Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP) advanced a proposal that could diminish legal protections of historic sites. The 16–5 vote approved revisions to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, a measure that mandates federal agencies to consider possible damages to historically significant sites before undertaking construction projects.

item.title: The Lost Pearls of New York City
item.description:
Walking down Pearl Street in lower Manhattan, you probably don’t realize that the name marks the original 17th-century East River shoreline of New York City. In fact, the street was named for a Lenape shell midden that was located on its southern section, which is also believed to have been adjacent to a Lenape canoe landing. It was one of many prominent middens that marked the region, and as Mark Kurlansky explains in his bestselling book The Big Oyster: History on the Half Shell (2006), middens are “the most common marker of a pre-European settlement anywhere in the area of the mouth of the Hudson.” These piles of oyster shells, he notes, were sometimes as much as four feet deep, sometimes buried in the ground, sometimes piled high.

The early 17th-century Dutch colonists were the first to note these large piles and many of them remained well into the 19th century when the last vestiges were dismantled and then used as filler for roads and other modernization projects. Brooklyn writer Daniel Tredwell wrote in his 1839 diary that he would explore these piles with his father:

 “On the way out we pass many Indian shell heaps bleached as white as snow, which they much resemble at a distance. Some of them on the banks of the creek extend from fifteen to thirty feet upon the bank, and under water, in many instances entirely across the creek. These shell heaps, long ere this, has excited our curiosity and we had proposed all manner of questioning concerning their authors. These questions my father did not and could not satisfactorily answer, and we were consequently unsatisfied, and hence there was a constantly recurring inquiry.”

The passage highlights that the erasure of Indigenous settlement was so thorough in 19th-century New York that it never occurred to the Tredwell family that the landmarks they visited were consciously created by those whom they displaced. 

That forgetting is at the foundation of Alan Michelson’s “The Oyster” project, which opened this past weekend on Governors Island and will continue until late fall. This history, Michelson’s public artwork suggests, is still present, and equally contested, as people who live here continue to ignore the mark that the oyster has on our daily lives.

item.title: Under Glass Cloches, Amber Cowan Nests Enchanting Flameworked Scenes
item.description:
Known for her lush assemblages of flameworked glass, Amber Cowan reimagines a ubiquitous yet fragile medium. Flowers, filigree, and colorful baubles cluster into dense compositions that invoke fairytale narratives and whimsical nature scenes. Cowan typically works with industrial scraps, antiques, and other offcasts, which allows her to draw on products and colorways that are no longer in production.

Currently leaning into cloche and coupe sculptures alongside her wall-based works, the Philadelphia-based artist is preparing for several upcoming exhibitions, including at San Francisco’s Museum of Craft and Design in September and Design Miami in December. Her work is on view now in The Passion of Collecting at The Baker Museum in Naples, Florida, and you can find more on Instagram.

item.title: Simone Forti in Her Own Words
item.description:
In 1961, Yoko Ono dedicated one of her famous screaming pieces to performance artist Simone Forti, who died in Los Angeles last week. That same year, Forti debuted her piece Five Dance Constructions and Some Other Things in Ono’s Manhattan loft. Just two years apart (with Ono being the elder), these two legends shared much in common. In a never-before-published interview with scholar and curator Julia Bryan-Wilson, Forti reflects on her history with Ono, aging, and her career over the decades with her typical charm and humility.

In the news, police arrest 16 protesters who carried portraits of people killed by ICE agents in a US Senate building. Also in DC, seven Smithsonian museums close because of a faulty cooling system. 

Also today: Artist Anna Boghiguian talks about her woven tapestries of Armenia's natural history, an artist is commissioned to reimagine Frieze London’s restrooms, and did you know that the harp is hot again? Read our weekly columns Art Movements and Required Reading for more. Happy Friday!

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Simone Forti Talks Yoko Ono, Dance, and Aging in Never-Before-Published Interview

About a dozen years ago, I happened to be simultaneously writing two different essays about two of the most influential artists of the 20th century who are almost exact contemporaries: Simone Forti (born in Italy in 1935) and Yoko Ono (born in Japan in 1933). Only two years apart, these women had many other things in common besides age: They were both transcultural migrants whose early lives were shaped by the deprivations of fascism and war. Both experienced discrimination — Forti’s Jewish family left Italy as a result of Mussolini’s Racial Laws, while Ono was (and still is) by turns exoticized and vilified as an Asian woman.

As cross-disciplinary groundbreakers, both Forti and Ono transgress the boundaries between sound, drawing, poetry, participation, movement, new media, and sculpture. They continually invoked touch as mode of connection, and they both incorporated everyday objects as charged collaborators. | Julia Bryan-Wilson

item.title: New York City’s Last Standing Wood Column Company Closes After 110 Years
item.description:
110 years ago, Thomas Lupo’s grandfather opened the American Wood Column Corporation in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood. Specializing in architectural woodwork including decorative moulding, columns, balusters, corbels, and more, the historic family-owned company is shutting down after more than a century. A new documentary directed and produced by filmmaker and photographer Joshua Charrow takes viewers on one final walk-through of the factory.

A vast collection of about 6,000 handmade wooden molds—many of them reverse carved molds—cover the walls and correspond to numbered samples for reference. “My grandfather bought these molds used, and they were used,” Lupo explains. “So they’ve got to be over 200 years old.”

Throughout the film, Charrow follows Lupo around the building, documenting the owner’s favorite pieces and timeless anecdotes. Among these works are six-foot pencils, ornamental department store columns, set designs from Saturday Night Live, grave details from The Godfather, The Exorcist stairway, and more.

Filled with family stories and nostalgic memories of growing up inside a woodworking studio, Lupo is cognizant of the fact that he, too, is growing older. His team, who has been with him for close to 40 years, believe it’s also time to retire gracefully. “I will be closing down the business. It’s not a question of if, it’s a question of when. That’s all.” he says. “Like anything else, everything changes. Time goes on.”

item.title: A Short Film Sheds Light on the Garfield Phones Washing Up on a French Beach Since the ’80s
item.description:
Amid the rugged, wave-churned shoreline of France’s Breton coast, a surprising tidbit of pop culture has kept beachcombers returning for more than 40 years. The short film “Silly Little Plastic Cat” transports us to this slice of Brittany, where local residents grew up collecting parts of a 1984 Garfield-themed plastic telephone on the beach—and still do. Photographer and director Zack Grant, founder the production studio 2020 Land, was intrigued by the story, which made news a few years back after the source of the dispersed merchandise was finally discovered.

The part of Brittany where the phones wash up is situated along a busy shipping thoroughfare. At some point during their transit in the mid-1980s, the shipping container carrying thousands of the units fell into the sea, and over the years, its spilled contents have continued to arrive in distinctively orange, tangled jumbles. As quirky as it is, the phenomenon also shines a light on the less humorous side: the vast quantity of garbage that washes ashore.

To put the scale of pollution into perspective, nearly 1,500 shipping containers were lost in 2025 alone. Less than 10 percent of those were recovered; the rest are still missing. It’s a small fraction of the hundreds of millions of containers transported annually, yet a single 40-foot container could hold the contents of an entire three- or four-bedroom house or around 400 mattresses. Multiply that by several hundred and consider everything we ship—clothing, medical supplies, car parts, you name it—and we can start to scratch the surface of the oceans’ staggering garbage patches.

“Silly Little Plastic Cat” illuminates the reality of pollution and also highlights how locals are motivated to help. Residents have adopted Garfield as something of a de facto mascot for cleanup projects. “We are 100 percent responsible for the current climate situation and current pollution,” says a local conservationist who aids in beach cleanups via Surfrider Foundation. “We are also actors in the solutions.” Another initiative invites people to work together to regenerate older or damaged items, making them usable once again while reducing consumption.

See more on Grant’s work on Vimeo.

item.title: Monumental Painted Wood Carvings by Jiang Miao Center Mindfulness
item.description:
The spiral is one of the most ubiquitous, universal symbols. Or perhaps it is more apt to describe the motif as mimicked from nature, where it occurs in the form of seashells, flowers, and curling waves. From Neolithic stone carvings at Newgrange in Ireland to swirling motifs on prehistoric pottery discovered in Thailand, the spiral represents growth, the cycles of life, and evolution. Sometimes two or more interlink, and other times they emerge from an endless line.

For artist Jiang Miao, Eastern philosophy is a touchstone. “The spiral symbolizes life, time, and the cyclical order of the universe, while color becomes a vessel for invisible energy beyond the material world,” says Whitestone Gallery, which presents the artist’s solo exhibition, Spiral of Energy.

Several series are represented in the show, including Heavenly Eyes, Mindfulness, Origin, and Taoist Trinity and the Self. “Heavenly Eyes proposes a perspective beyond ordinary human vision, contemplating the essence of existence and the order of the universe, while Mindfulness explores the nature of life through introspection and awakened consciousness,” the gallery says. Taoist Trinity and the Self is all tondos and emphasizes perpetualness. They can also be monumental: one reaches about seven feet in diameter.

Miao meticulously carves intricate textures into wood panels, then applies vibrant acrylic paint to create a sensorial movement, contrast, and glow. Both the approach and result are inherently concerned with time and concentration, spirituality and mindfulness.

Spiral of Energy continues through August 23 in Seoul. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

item.title: Nuart Aberdeen 2026: Poetry In The Streets
item.description: Welcome to the latest edition of Nuart Aberdeen. As far as we can ascertain, this will be the first street art festival in the world with a focus primarily on poetry and text-based works. Over the years, for better or worse, the large scale colourful figurative mural has come to dominate the culture we work with, and although it’s an aspect of the culture we support, due to the resources required to produce murals, they’re perhaps also the least democratic form of art on the streets.
